source_type: UN agency guidance and case studies
community_problem: Health facilities lack safe water, sanitation, hygiene, waste management, and cleaning practices.
intervention: Develop national WASH roadmaps and targets
evidence_summary: WHO/UNICEF identify eight practical steps for improving WASH in health care facilities, illustrated with country examples and case studies.
recommended_transfer: Assess water, sanitation, hygiene, waste, and cleaning gaps
Set simple local improvement targets
Create a facility/community maintenance plan
Engage health workers and local community groups
Track progress monthly
urgent_warning: For severe illness, dehydration, persistent vomiting, infants, elderly, pregnant people, or outbreak-like symptoms, contact qualified healthcare workers immediately.
limitations: Guidance must be adapted to local facility type, water access, budget, and government health protocols.

source_type: UN SDG success stories and lessons learned
community_problem: Communities need practical examples of SDG interventions that can be scaled or replicated.
evidence_summary: UN DESA curated SDG good practices and lessons learned, emphasizing how practices can be scaled and replicated worldwide.
recommended_transfer: Match the local problem to a similar SDG good practice
Check whether the required partners and resources exist locally
Start with a small pilot before scaling
Document results and barriers
urgent_warning: Do not copy interventions blindly; validate cultural, environmental, legal, and safety fit locally.
limitations: Good practices are high-level and may need additional local operational details.

source_type: UN-linked sustainable development case study database
community_problem: Local communities need examples of how sustainable development problems were addressed through partnerships.
evidence_summary: The SDG Fund case-study database collects best practices on how to advance SDGs through partnerships across UN agencies, governments, academia, civil society, and business.
recommended_transfer: Identify stakeholders affected by the problem
Map existing local organizations and government contacts
Choose one intervention pattern from a similar case
Define simple indicators before action
urgent_warning: For health, food, water, or safety risks, involve qualified local professionals rather than relying only on app suggestions.
limitations: Case-study applicability depends on local governance, funding, and community acceptance.

source_name: World Bank Water and Sanitation Program
community_problem: Urban low-income communities lack affordable, safe, and sustainable sanitation services.
evidence_summary: The World Bank report discusses community slum sanitation in India and focuses on affordable, safe, and sustainable water and sanitation access for poor communities.
recommended_transfer: Map sanitation gaps by lane/household cluster
Identify public toilet/service access and maintenance gaps
Coordinate with municipality or urban local body
Plan maintenance and user accountability
Track complaints, usage, cleanliness, and water availability
urgent_warning: If sewage exposure, diarrheal illness, or unsafe toilet conditions affect children or vulnerable people, contact local health/sanitation authorities.
limitations: Urban sanitation models may not transfer directly to rural villages without adaptation.

source_type: Water supply and sanitation case studies in India
community_problem: Poor water and sanitation services create unequal burdens, especially for women and socially excluded groups.
evidence_summary: The World Bank document describes Indian case studies on improving water supply and sanitation services and highlights gender and social exclusion dimensions.
recommended_transfer: Collect separate feedback from women, girls, elderly, and marginalized groups
Check safety, distance, timing, and affordability of services
Engage local service providers
Create a complaint and tracking mechanism
urgent_warning: If sanitation access creates safety risks for women or children, escalate to local authorities/community protection structures.
limitations: Requires local social context and gender-sensitive consultation before implementation.

community_problem: Workers and nearby communities need safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services at work and home.
evidence_summary: WaterAid’s India tea-estate work focused on improving WASH services and hygiene behaviours for employees and their communities while building evidence for investment.
recommended_transfer: Assess WASH access at workplaces and homes
Install or improve handwashing and sanitation facilities
Run hygiene behavior sessions
Track absenteeism, illness complaints, water access, and facility use
urgent_warning: Workplace/community health issues should be escalated through local health and labor/safety channels when severe.
limitations: Tea-estate workplace patterns may need adaptation for villages, schools, factories, or informal settlements.

community_problem: Low-income families face barriers to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services.
evidence_summary: WaterAid’s learning module describes an equity and inclusion WASH services approach for low-income families within urban WASH systems strengthening.
recommended_transfer: Identify who is excluded from WASH access
Assess affordability, distance, disability access, and safety
Prioritize low-income households
Coordinate with government/NGO service providers
urgent_warning: Do not recommend infrastructure changes without checking land, safety, and government rules.
limitations: Training-module guidance must be localized with local WASH actors.

community_problem: Communities and facilities need practical steps to improve WASH in health-care settings.
evidence_summary: The resource outlines WHO/UNICEF practical steps and examples from countries that have implemented WASH in health care facility actions.
recommended_transfer: Start with a basic facility WASH assessment
Choose one priority gap: water, toilets, hand hygiene, waste, cleaning
Assign responsibility and timeline
Review progress regularly
urgent_warning: Infection-control and medical-waste issues require trained health facility leadership and official protocols.
limitations: Country examples are not direct prescriptions; local facility conditions matter.
